title: Sandu: The Three Poisons 4
content:
Wei Wuxian’s heart leaped into his throat. Were we spotted? Run now, or hold still?

Right then, soft sniffling drifted from behind the compound wall. Amidst heavy, shuffling footsteps, a man's voice wheedled gently, "Don't cry, baby. You're ruining your pretty makeup."

Wei Wuxian and Jiang Cheng knew that voice down to their bones—Wen Chao!

Wang Lingjiao whimpered back, "Will you stop liking me if my face gets ruined?"

"How could I? Jiaojiao, I’ll adore you no matter what you look like."

"I was so terrified..." she sobbed, laying it on thick. "Today... I honestly thought that bitch was going to kill me. I thought I’d never see you again... Wen-gongzi... I..."

Rustling fabric hinted that Wen Chao had swept her into an embrace. "Shh, it's over, Jiaojiao. You're safe now. Thank goodness Wen Zhuliu watched your back."

Wang Lingjiao pouted, her voice laced with venom. "Why do you keep bringing him up? I despise that Wen Zhuliu. If he hadn't dragged his feet, I wouldn't have taken a single blow! My face is still throbbing—it hurts so bad..."

She was the one who had driven Wen Zhuliu away so he wouldn't cramp her style, walking right into her own beating, yet here she was twisting the truth without missing a beat. Still, Wen Chao loved nothing more than when she played the petulant damsel. "There, there, let me kiss it better... Hate him all you want, but don't push him too far. The man's cultivation is monstrous. Father has praised his rare talent more than once, and I still plan on keeping him around to do my heavy lifting for years to come."

"Talent..." Wang Lingjiao scoffed. "So what if he's talented? Wen-zongzhu has legions of brilliant cultivators under his command—tens of thousands of them! Would losing one dog really bring the heavens down?"

She was openly nudging Wen Chao to punish Wen Zhuliu to soothe her bruised ego, but Wen Chao only chuckled. As much as he doted on her, he wasn't stupid enough to sacrifice an elite bodyguard for a concubine's whim. Wen Zhuliu had deflected countless assassination attempts, kept his mouth shut, and stayed fiercely loyal to Wen Ruohan—which meant he’d never turn on Wen Chao, either. Such a loyal, lethal weapon was irreplaceable. Sensing his indifference, Wang Lingjiao pressed harder: "Look at him! He's just a grunt under your thumb, yet he struts around acting above his station! When I went to slap that Yu bitch's corpse, he actually had the nerve to stop me! She was already dead—just cold meat! Looking down on me like that... isn't he looking down on you?"

Jiang Cheng’s grip slipped, his boots sliding against the brick. Wei Wuxian’s hand shot out, catching him by the scruff just in time.

Both of them choked back hot, silent tears that spilled over their cheeks, dripping down their knuckles and pattering into the dirt.

Wei Wuxian couldn't help but remember Jiang Fengmian leaving this morning after that bitter spat with Madam Yu. The final words they’d exchanged had carried no warmth, only sharp edges. Did they ever get to see each other one last time? Did Jiang Fengmian ever get the chance to say another word to his wife?

Wen Chao snorted dismissively on the other side of the wall. "That's just his bizarre quirk. Always going on about how a gentleman may be killed but not humiliated. He’s the one who slit her throat—preaching chivalry over a corpse is ridiculous."

Wang Lingjiao chimed in eagerly, "Exactly! Total hypocrite!"

Basking in her flattery, Wen Chao let out a booming laugh. Wang Lingjiao sneered, "Honestly, that Yu bitch had it coming. Back in the day, she used her clan’s muscle to force a man to marry her. And what did she get for it? Even with a ring on her finger, he never loved her. A discarded wife for over ten years, the laughingstock of the cultivation world behind closed doors. And she still didn't know how to keep her head down—arrogant to the end. Serves her right."

"Is that so?" Wen Chao mused. "She was quite the looker, though. Why didn't Jiang Fengmian want a piece of that?"

In his shallow mind, as long as a woman was pretty, a man had no reason to turn his nose up. The only women deserving contempt were the plain ones and the ones who refused to warm his bed.

Wang Lingjiao replied, "Use your head! She was utterly overbearing. A woman running around lashing people with whips and slapping faces, totally lacking in basic manners. Jiang Fengmian married that nightmare and got dragged into the mud with her—eight lifetimes of rotten luck, if you ask me."

"Damn right!" Wen Chao agreed heartily. "A woman should be like my Jiaojiao—sweet, obedient, tender, and totally devoted to me."

Wang Lingjiao dissolved into giggles. Listening to this filthy banter, Wei Wuxian trembled with a dizzying cocktail of grief and rage. He braced for Jiang Cheng to snap, but Jiang Cheng hung limp, entirely numb, as if shock had stolen his consciousness.

Wang Lingjiao purred, "Of course I'm devoted to you... who else would I ever lean on?"

Just then, a hurried voice broke in from the yard: "Wen-gongzi! Every room has been swept. We've cataloged over twenty-four hundred spiritual treasures, and the men are sorting them now."

Those were Lotus Pier’s treasures. The Jiang Clan’s heritage!

Wen Chao threw his head back, howling with laughter. "Excellent! Tonight calls for a grand celebration. Throw a banquet right here in the main hall. Waste nothing!"

Wang Lingjiao chimed in sweetly, "Congratulations on taking Lotus Pier, gongzi."

"What 'Lotus Pier'?" Wen Chao barked. "Scrape that name off the gates! Tear down every door bearing their nine-petaled lotus and carve the Qishan Wen sunburst over them! Jiaojiao, dance for me—show me your best moves!"

Wei Wuxian and Jiang Cheng couldn't stomach another second. They dropped from the wall, their boots stumbling blindly through the dark as they fled Lotus Pier. Even after putting miles between them and the estate, the hollow cheers of that rabble refused to fade, accompanied by a woman’s lilting, celebratory singing drifting above the lake—slicing into their ears and hearts like a jagged, poisoned blade.

After sprinting for miles without pause, Jiang Cheng skidded to a halt.

Wei Wuxian pulled up beside him. When Jiang Cheng pivoted on his heel to head straight back, Wei Wuxian lunged, grabbing his arm. "Jiang Cheng, what are you doing?! Don't go back!"

Jiang Cheng violently wrenched his sleeve away. "Don't go back?! Are you even listening to yourself?! You want me to just walk away?! My parents' bodies are rotting on that training ground! How can I just run?! If I don't go back, where the hell am I supposed to go?!"

Wei Wuxian tightened his grip, digging his fingers in. "What can you possibly do right now?! They butchered Uncle Jiang and Madam Yu—going back is pure suicide!"

Jiang Cheng roared, "Then I'll die! If you're that terrified of death, get lost! Don't stand in my way!"

Wei Wuxian clamped both hands around his shoulders, wrestling him down. "Revenge is a dish best served cold! We will take their bodies back, but not tonight!"

Jiang Cheng twisted out of the hold, swinging a fist into his ribs. "If not now, when?! I'm sick of your face—get the fuck out of my way!"

Wei Wuxian barked back, "Uncle Jiang and Madam Yu told me to watch over you! They told me to keep you safe!"

"Shut up!" Jiang Cheng shoved him with all his might, his voice cracking into a desperate shriek. "Why?!"

The blow sent Wei Wuxian crashing backward into the tall grass. Jiang Cheng threw himself on top of him, snatching his collar and violently shaking him. "Why?! Why did this happen?! Why?! Are you happy now?! Are you satisfied?!"

His fingers clamped around Wei Wuxian’s throat, his eyes shot through with broken crimson veins. "Why did you have to save Lan Wangji?!"

Drowning in blinding grief and fury, Jiang Cheng had completely lost his mind, all control slipping through his fingers. Wei Wuxian clawed at his wrists. "Jiang Cheng..."

Jiang Cheng pinned him into the dirt, howling into his face, "Why did you have to save him?! Why did you always have to play the hero?! How many times did I tell you to keep your head down?! Not to cause trouble! Not to stick your neck out! Did you love playing the martyr that much?! You see where playing hero got us now, don't you?! Huh?! Are you happy now?!"

"So what if Lan Wangji and Jin Zixuan died?! You should have let them rot! Their lives had nothing to do with us! What did their deaths have to do with our family?! Why us?! Why did we have to pay for them?!"

"Die... just die, why didn't you all just die?! Go to hell, every last one of you!!!"

Suffocating, his face flushing a dangerous scarlet, Wei Wuxian finally roared, "Jiang Cheng!!!"

The hands locked around his windpipe suddenly went limp.

Jiang Cheng stared down at him, tears pouring unchecked down his face. From the bottom of his chest tore a strangled, dying wail—a wretched, broken sob.

"I want my parents back..." he wept, his voice cracking like splintered glass. "Give them back to me..."

He was begging Wei Wuxian for his mother and father. But no matter who he begged, the dead were not coming home.

Tears spilled from Wei Wuxian’s eyes, too. The two boys sat crumpled in the tall weeds, staring at each other through blurred, grief-stricken sobs.

Deep down, Jiang Cheng knew the truth: even if Wei Wuxian hadn't stepped in to save Lan Wangji in the cave of the Xuanwu of Slaughter, the Wen Clan would have found an excuse to bring fire and ruin to their doorstep sooner or later. Yet a tiny, agonizing sliver of him couldn't let go of the thought that if Wei Wuxian hadn't acted, maybe disaster wouldn't have struck this fast. Maybe there would have been room to breathe, room to maneuver.

It was that cruel, desperate 'what if' that poisoned his marrow with helpless fury and bitter regret, tearing his heart to ribbons.

By the time the first pale light of dawn cracked the horizon, Jiang Cheng had gone entirely hollow.

He had actually drifted off a few times through the night. First from sheer exhaustion, his body giving out after crying itself raw. Second, because he clung desperately to the hope that this was all a sickening nightmare—that if he just shut his eyes and woke up, he’d find himself back in his own bed at Lotus Pier. His father would be sitting in the courtyard, polishing his sword over an open book; his mother would be snapping at Wei Wuxian’s ridiculous faces; his sister would be daydreaming by the stove, plotting what delicious soup to brew for dinner; and his shidis would be skipping their morning drills to chase each other over the boardwalks.

Instead, the biting night wind had frozen his limbs, waking him with a blinding migraine in the weeds, curled behind a desolate, barren hillside.

Wei Wuxian was the first to stir.

Bracing his hands against his thighs, he dragged himself upright, his voice sandpaper-rough. "Let's move."

Jiang Cheng didn't budge. Wei Wuxian reached down to take his hand. "Come on. Let's go."

"...Where?" Jiang Cheng rasped, his throat parched.

"Meishan. To the Yu Clan, to find Shijie."

Jiang Cheng slapped his hand away. After a heavy beat, he pushed himself up, climbing slowly to his feet.

They turned toward Meishan, traveling strictly on foot.

Every step felt like hauling a mountain on their backs, their bodies running on sheer fumes.

Jiang Cheng walked with his chin pinned to his chest, his right hand clutched over his heart, ceaselessly tracing the smooth band of Zidian coiled around his index finger—the sole surviving relic of his family. Every few paces, he looked back over his shoulder toward Lotus Pier, staring longingly at the place that was once his home, now reduced to a den of vipers. Again and again, as if he could never look enough, as if nursing one last ember of impossible hope. And every single time, fresh tears broke free and tracked down his grime-streaked face.

They had fled in a panic without provisions. Running on empty since yesterday, after half a day of trekking, dark spots danced across their vision. Leaving the desolate countryside behind, they stumbled into a small border town. Wei Wuxian glanced at Jiang Cheng, whose hollow, leaden exhaustion made it clear he couldn't take another step. "Sit here," Wei Wuxian instructed. "I'll scavenge some food."

Jiang Cheng offered no reply, not even a nod. Across the entire trek, he had barely uttered three words.

Wei Wuxian reminded him to stay put once more before turning into the market. He had always made a habit of stashing loose change in random pockets, a quirk that proved to be a lifesaver now. Circling the stalls, he bought a bundle of hot buns, flatbreads, and dried rations for the long road ahead, rushing back in less than half an incense stick.

Jiang Cheng was gone.

Clutching his armful of steamed bread and fruit, panic seized Wei Wuxian’s chest. Forcing himself to breathe, he scoured the immediate street, but found no trace of him. Terror finally broke through his calm. Grabbing an old cobbler working at the corner, he blurted out, "Lao-bo, there was a young master sitting right here just a minute ago—did you see where he went?!"

The cobbler smoothed a thick thread between his lips. "The lad who was with you earlier?"

"Yes! Him!"

"I had my head down with work, so I didn't see clearly," the old man mumbled. "He was staring off into space watching the crowd for a while, and when I looked up again, he’d vanished. Probably walked off."

Wei Wuxian whispered in horror, "...Walked off... He went back..."

He went back to Lotus Pier to steal their bodies!

Like a madman, Wei Wuxian spun on his heel and bolted, sprinting down the road they had just come from.

The heavy rations dragging on his arms quickly proved a hindrance; after a short sprint, he hurled the bundle into the dirt. But before he made it another mile, dark spots swarmed his vision, his drained core giving out. Weak-kneed and suffocating with panic, he crashed face-first into the dirt road.

The fall threw dust across his teeth, the dry, metallic taste of earth coating his tongue.

A crushing, suffocating wave of utter powerlessness and boiling rage tore through his chest. He slammed his fist into the gravel with an agonized roar before forcing himself back onto his feet. Stumbling back to where he’d dropped the food, he wiped the dirt off a steamed bun, shoved it into his mouth, and choked it down in two massive bites—chewing as if tearing through raw flesh, the dry bread scraping down his throat so hard his chest burned. He stuffed a few more into his tunic, gnawing on another as he ran, desperate to intercept Jiang Cheng along the road.

Yet by the time he reached the outskirts of Lotus Pier, the moon hung high and cold in a star-speckled sky, and he hadn't crossed Jiang Cheng's path once.

Staring at the blazing lanterns illuminating Lotus Pier from afar, Wei Wuxian braced his hands on his knees, gasping for air. The metallic tang of blood welling up from his lungs coated his mouth, his vision dimming into dark tunnels.

How did I miss him? he thought frantically. Even running on fumes, that was my top speed. He was more exhausted than I was, crushed by twice the grief—how could he have run faster than me? Did he actually come back here? If not Lotus Pier, where else could he go? Would he head to Meishan alone, leaving me behind?

Taking a few steady breaths to rein in his ragged core, he decided to scout the compound first. Creeping along the base of the perimeter wall, a desperate prayer echoed in his skull: Please, gods, let no one be gossiping about Jiang Cheng’s corpse in the courtyard tonight. If they are... if they are, I'll...

If they are, what could I even do?

Nothing. He was utterly helpless. Lotus Pier was in ruins, Jiang Fengmian and Madam Yu were gone, and Jiang Cheng had vanished. He was entirely on his own—unarmed, stripped of his sword, clueless, and weak.

For the first time in his life, he realized how tiny and insignificant he truly was. Standing against the colossal juggernaut of the Qishan Wen Clan, he was nothing more than a mantis trying to stop a war chariot with its frail arms.

Tears burned at the corners of his eyes, threatening to spill over again. Rounding a corner of the wall, a silhouette draped in the sunburst robes suddenly turned into his path.

Like a coiled spring, Wei Wuxian struck!

In a flash, his left hand locked both of the stranger's wrists behind his back while his right clamped firmly around his throat. Forcing his voice into the lowest, most feral growl he could muster, he hissed, "Don't make a sound! One twitch and I'll snap your neck!"

Pinned against the masonry, the captive stammered in a breathless panic, "W-Wei-gongzi! It's me, it's me!"

The voice belonged to a youth. Wei Wuxian’s first thought flared: An undercover ally hiding in Wen colors?

Yet the voice was entirely foreign. Quashing the thought, his grip tightened, cutting off the air. "Don't play games with me!"

"I-I'm not playing games!" the youth wheezed. "Wei-gongzi, y-you can look at my face!"

Look at his face? Wei Wuxian thought, suspicious. Is he going to spit blinding powder at me?

Keeping his guard up, he wrenched the boy's jaw around. The youth had clean, delicate features and a soft, youthful handsomeness—the very same Wen junior they’d glimpsed when peeking over the wall yesterday.

Wei Wuxian’s heart went stone-cold. "I don't know you."

He shoved the boy's head back toward the stone, his fingers digging into his windpipe. "Who are you?!"

A trace of dejection flickered across the youth's face. "I... I am Wen Ning."

Wei Wuxian frowned. "Who the hell is Wen Ning?" Yet his brain calculated quickly: Doesn't matter who he is. As long as he holds rank, he might make decent hostage collateral to trade for Jiang Cheng!

Wen Ning mumbled, "I... a few years back, at the Qishan Discussion Conference... I... archery..."

Listening to him stammer, impatience scorched through Wei Wuxian. "Spit it out! Are you a stutterer?!"

Wen Ning flinched under his hand, looking ready to cover his head and drop into a protective squat. He whispered meekly, "Y-Yes..."

Looking at this timid, stuttering boy shrinking like a bruised pup, something clicked in Wei Wuxian's memory. The Qishan conference two years ago... the archery competition... Wait, there was someone like that!

Wei Wuxian tested the waters. "You're that... Wen... Wen-whatever, the one with the decent aim?"

Wen Ning nodded frantically, a flicker of joy lighting up his eyes. "Y-Yes, that's me! Yesterday... I saw you and Jiang-gongzi by the wall. I figured you might come back..."

Wei Wuxian froze. "You saw me yesterday?"

"Y-Yes."

"You saw me, and you didn't raise the alarm?"

"Never!" Wen Ning blurted out. "I would never tell them!"

For once, he didn't stutter, his tone ringing with the absolute weight of a sacred vow. Suspicion and bewilderment warred in Wei Wuxian's chest.

Wen Ning pressed on, "Wei-gongzi, you came back for Jiang-gongzi, right?"

Wei Wuxian snapped, "Is Jiang Cheng inside?!"

Wen Ning answered honestly, "Yes. He was dragged back yesterday."

Wei Wuxian’s mind spun into overdrive: Jiang Cheng is inside; I have to breach Lotus Pier. Use Wen Ning as a shield? Useless—Wen Chao probably looks down on this kid anyway, an exchange won't work! And is he lying to me? He's a Wen! But he didn't rat us out yesterday... If I let him go, will he sell me out the second I turn my back? Could a Wen dog truly possess a shred of decency? If I want to guarantee zero leaks, the only way is...

A spark of killing intent flickered in Wei Wuxian's eyes.

He was not a man who loved bloodshed, but having his home reduced to a slaughterhouse had stoked an inferno in his chest. In these desperate straits, mercy was a luxury he couldn't afford. A single snap of his wrist, and Wen Ning’s neck would be broken!

Amidst his chaotic thoughts, Wen Ning spoke up softly: "Wei-gongzi, are you here to break him out?"

Wei Wuxian’s fingers curled tight against the skin. "What else?"

Wen Ning managed an anxious, tentative smile. "I knew it. I... I can help you get him out."

Wei Wuxian stared, convinced his ears were playing tricks on him. "...You? You want to help me break him out?!"

"Yes," Wen Ning nodded eagerly. "R-Right now. I can bring him out this second. Wen Chao and his inner circle just left!"

Wei Wuxian gripped his shoulder. "You really can?!"

"I can! I... I'm technically a Wen disciple, and I have a squad of men who listen to me."

Wei Wuxian's tone went sharp as a blade: "Listen to you? Listen to you murder people?!"

Wen Ning waved his hands frantically. "N-No, no! My men never kill recklessly! I haven't harmed a single soul from the Jiang Clan either! I only heard about Lotus Pier after the fact and rushed here as fast as I could. Truly!"

Wei Wuxian stared hard into his eyes. What is his angle? A trap? Buying time? But this lie is so absurd no sane spy would spin it! Does he take me for a fool?!

Yet terrifyingly, deep down in his hollow chest, an irrational, wild surge of desperate hope flared to life.

He cursed himself inwardly—calling himself an idiot, naive, pathetic, clinging to pipe dreams. But he was completely alone. No sword, no spiritual talismans, facing hundreds of stationed Wen cultivators and the Core-Melting Hand himself.

He wasn't afraid of dying. He was terrified of dying before he could drag Jiang Cheng out of that hell, breaking his sacred vow to Jiang Fengmian and Madam Yu. In this hopeless corner, the only lifeline he had left was a Wen boy he had crossed paths with exactly three times in his entire life!

Wei Wuxian licked his dry lips, his voice trembling faintly. "Then... can you... can you help me... help me retrieve the bodies of Jiang-zongzhu and Madam Yu...?"

Without realizing it, he had begun to stutter, too. Halfway through, remembering he was still pinning Wen Ning in a lethal chokehold, he awkwardly released his grip. Yet his fingers stayed coiled; if Wen Ning bolted or cried for help, he would cave his skull in instantly.

Instead, Wen Ning simply turned around, his eyes earnest and clear. "I... I will do everything I can."

Wei Wuxian waited in a daze. Pacing in frantic circles, his thoughts spiraled: What is wrong with me? Have I lost my mind? Why would a Wen help me? Why am I betting our lives on him? What if he’s leading me into an ambush and Jiang Cheng isn't even in there? No—it would be a blessing if Jiang Cheng wasn't in there!

Before half an incense stick had burned, Wen Ning silently stepped out of the shadows, carrying a body slung over his back.

The figure was coated in dried blood, his face deathly pale, eyes locked shut, hanging limp across Wen Ning’s shoulders. It was Jiang Cheng.

Wei Wuxian lunged forward, whispering frantically, "Jiang Cheng?! Jiang Cheng?!"

Reaching out, he checked the pulse at his neck. Still breathing. Wen Ning extended an open palm, dropping a silver ring into Wei Wuxian's hand. "Jiang-gongzi's Zidian. I brought it out."

Words failed Wei Wuxian completely. Remembering that he had contemplated murdering this boy moments ago, all he could manage was a hoarse, humbled whisper: "...Thank you!"

Wen Ning shook his head softly. "No need... The remains of Jiang-xiansheng and Madam Yu... I’ve had my men discreetly move them out of the compound. I’ll hand them over once we're safe. Th-This place isn't safe. We must run..."

He didn't need to say it twice. Wei Wuxian took Jiang Cheng, preparing to hoist him onto his own back, only for his eyes to snag on a savage, crisscrossing crimson gash torn across Jiang Cheng’s chest.

Wei Wuxian gasped, "The Discipline Whip?!"

Wen Ning nodded solemnly. "Yes. Wen Chao got his hands on the Jiang Clan's whip... Jiang-gongzi has other injuries, too."

Wei Wuxian gave his torso a cursory check—at least three broken ribs, and gods knew how much internal trauma lay hidden beneath his skin.

Wen Ning continued, "Once Wen Chao returns and discovers he's gone, he’ll scour all of Yunmeng to hunt you down... Wei-gongzi, if you trust me, I can... I can take you somewhere to hide first."

Jiang Cheng was in critical condition, desperately needing medicine and a quiet place to mend. Running blindly through the wilderness, starving and hunted, was a death sentence. They were utterly cornered, backed into a dead end; aside from leaning on Wen Ning, Wei Wuxian had no other moves left to play.

Yesterday, he would have scoffed at the idea of running to a Wen for salvation, preferring to die on his feet. But right now, all Wei Wuxian could say was, "Thank you!"

Wen Ning waved his hands frantically. "N-No... please don't. Wei-gongzi, this way. I... I have a boat prepared..."

Hoisting Jiang Cheng onto his back, Wei Wuxian followed Wen Ning to a skiff hidden among the reeds. Once they laid Jiang Cheng down in the shelter of the cabin, Wen Ning efficiently began cleaning his wounds, dressing the lacerations with medicinal paste. Watching the boy's skilled, practiced hands, Wei Wuxian couldn't help but recall the very first time they’d met at the grand Qishan Discussion Conference.

It was the year he, Lan Wangji, Lan Xichen, and Jin Zixuan had claimed the top four ranks in archery.

Before the tournament kicked off that day, Wei Wuxian had been wandering aimlessly through the sprawling courtyards of Nightless City. Idling past an ornamental garden, the sharp, rhythmic twang of a bowstring caught his ear.

Parting the branches, he saw a youth in plain white robes standing in a clearing, drawing his bow toward a distant target, smoothly loosing the string.

The boy's profile was clean and delicate, his posture textbook-perfect. The target's red bullseye was already bristling with a dense cluster of fletchings, and this new arrow drilled straight into the center with surgical precision.

A perfect record—not a single stray shot.

Wei Wuxian cheered from the brush, "Brilliant marksmanship!"

Having just landed the shot, the boy reached into his quiver for another arrow, only to jump out of his skin at the sudden voice. His hand trembled, dropping the arrow into the dirt.

Wei Wuxian stepped out from the flowers with an easy grin. "Which young master of the Wen Clan are you? Fantastic shot, truly impressive! I’ve never seen anyone in your family shoot so—"

Before he could finish, the boy had abandoned his bow and bolted into the trees, vanishing like a startled rabbit.

Wei Wuxian stood there, rubbing his chin in amused bewilderment. Am I that handsome? Handsome enough to scare people away?

He brushed it off as an odd encounter and sauntered back to the main plaza. With the competition about to begin, the Wen pavilion was locked in an uproar. Wei Wuxian nudged Jiang Cheng. "Why does their clan turn every event into a circus? What's the drama today?"

Jiang Cheng scoffed, "What else? Spots on the roster are limited, and they're bickering over who gets to shoot." He added with blatant contempt, "Every last one of those Wen bastards shoots like garbage anyway. What difference does it make who takes the field?"

Across the yard, Wen Chao barked, "One more! We need one more to fill the roster! Last spot!"

Standing near the edge of the crowd was the very same white-robed youth from the garden. Glancing nervously left and right, he summoned every ounce of courage he possessed to tentatively raise his hand. But his arm was barely lifted, and unlike the others, he didn't dare shout his own name. After being jostled around by the rowdy mob, someone finally noticed him, blinking in surprise. "Qionglin? Even you want to enter?"

The boy called Qionglin nodded meekly, only for another disciple to laugh in his face: "Nobody's ever seen you hold a bow! Why waste a slot? Stop daydreaming."

Wen Qionglin opened his mouth to defend himself, but the man waved him off: "Enough, don't waste our time trying to be trendy. Our scores will be tallied; if you go up there and humiliate us, don't come crying to me."

Wei Wuxian thought, Humiliate you? If anyone in your useless clan has a chance of salvaging your dignity, it's him.

The arrogant dismissal rubbed Wei Wuxian entirely the wrong way. Raising his voice, he called out across the plaza: "Who says he's never held a bow?! He shoots, and he's damn good at it!"

The crowd turned in surprise, trading glances between Wei Wuxian and the boy. Wen Qionglin’s pale face flushed crimson under the sudden spotlight, his dark eyes staring wide at Wei Wuxian. Hands tucked behind his back, Wei Wuxian sauntered over. "Didn't you just shoot brilliantly in the garden?"

Wen Chao looked over, deeply skeptical. "Really? You're good? How come I've never heard of this?"

Wen Qionglin stammered softly, "...I... I only picked it up recently..."

His voice was so quiet and halting it sounded like it could be snuffed out at any moment—and indeed, people routinely talked over him. Wen Chao cut him off with an impatient wave: "Fine, there's a target over there. Take a shot right now. If it's good, you're on the team; if it's trash, get lost."

The crowd parted, leaving an empty circle around Wen Qionglin. Gripping his bow with white knuckles, he cast anxious, pleading glances around the yard. Seeing his crippling lack of confidence, Wei Wuxian stepped up, clapping a hand on his shoulder. "Relax. Just shoot like you did earlier."

Wen Qionglin gave him a look of profound gratitude, drew in a shaky breath, and raised his bow.

Yet the moment the string drew back, Wei Wuxian winced inwardly. Uh-oh.

The boy had clearly never fired a shot in front of an audience in his life. His fingers and forearms shook violently; when the string snapped forward, the arrow flew wild, missing the target entirely.

The surrounding Wen disciples erupted into mocking laughter.

"Call that good?!"
"I could beat that with my eyes shut!"
"Stop wasting time, pick someone who actually knows how to hold a weapon!"

Flushing red all the way to his ears, Wen Qionglin didn't wait to be dismissed; he turned on his heel and fled in mortified shame.

Wei Wuxian jogged after him. "Hey, wait up! Qionglin-xiong, right? Why are you running?!"

Hearing the call, Wen Qionglin skidded to a halt, turning around with his chin pinned to his collarbones, radiating pure misery. "...I'm sorry."

Wei Wuxian blinked. "What are you apologizing to me for?"

"You... you vouched for me," Wen Qionglin mumbled, his voice thick with guilt. "And I... I embarrassed you..."

Wei Wuxian laughed. "What's there to embarrass me? You don't usually shoot in front of people, do you? Got stage fright?"

Wen Qionglin nodded meekly.

Wei Wuxian smiled. "Have some faith in yourself. To be blunt, you shoot circles around the rest of your clan. Among all the young masters I've seen, there are at most three people whose archery beats yours."

Jiang Cheng caught up, scowling. "What are you doing over here? Three whats?"

Wei Wuxian pointed at him. "Take this guy, for instance—he can't shoot as well as you."

Jiang Cheng flared, "You looking for a beating?!"

Taking Jiang Cheng's shove in stride, Wei Wuxian continued smoothly, "I mean it. There's nothing to be nervous about; practice in front of crowds a few more times and you'll get used to it. Next time, you'll blow everyone away."

This Wen Qionglin was clearly a distant branch disciple, holding an awkward, middling status in the clan—timid, insecure, and clumsy with words. He had poured blood and sweat into honing his craft, finally gathering the courage to enter the arena, only to choke under pressure. Without a little encouragement, this gentle soul might crawl into a shell and never pick up a bow again. Wei Wuxian gave him a few reassuring pointers, correcting a couple of minor flaws he’d noticed back in the garden. Wen Qionglin listened with rapt attention, hanging onto every word, nodding fervently.

Jiang Cheng snapped, "Quit running your mouth! The tournament is starting, get your ass to the staging grounds!"

Turning back, Wei Wuxian said with deadpan seriousness, "I'm heading into the ring now. Watch closely later and see how it's done..."

Jiang Cheng hauled him away by the collar, muttering, "Watch what? You think you're some grand role model?!"

Wei Wuxian pondered it, blinking innocently. "Well... aren't I?"

"Wei Wuxian! Nobody has less shame than you!"

...

Pulling his mind back to the present, Wei Wuxian shifted his gaze from Wen Ning to the blood-drenched, unconscious form of Jiang Cheng, his knuckles white as his fists clenched tight.

They traveled by water first, drifting downstream before transferring to a carriage Wen Ning had arranged along the road.

By the following day, they reached Yiling.
